title: Sharp variance and functional limits for thinned counts in infinite birth–death chains
shortTitle: When event counts have a Brownian limit
oneLine: An exact edge-energy criterion separates finite from divergent stationary variance rates, with functional limits and a joint-count covariance extension.
abstract: This unrefereed candidate treats independently retained jumps of nonexplosive, irreducible, positive recurrent continuous-time birth–death chains with finite retained intensity. A cumulative edge-energy series gives the exact finite-versus-infinite stationary variance-rate boundary without requiring square-integrable intensity or finite mean raw activity. Finite energy yields a functional central limit theorem from every fixed initial distribution; variance convergence requires additional control of that distribution. A multivariate extension gives explicit covariance for correlated detections at the same jump, and worked examples separate weak convergence from convergence of moments.

problem.name: Infinite-state extension of thinned birth–death counts

keyResults: The stationary variance rate is finite exactly when a cumulative edge-energy series converges; otherwise variance divided by time diverges.
Finite energy gives a Brownian functional limit from every fixed initial probability law.
A heavy-tailed starting distribution can have infinite variance at every positive time despite the weak functional limit.
Joint counts allow dependent marks at the same jump, with an explicit covariance matrix separating shared-chain effects from simultaneous detection.

narration: When event counts have a Brownian limit. An Evidence Press briefing. Imagine a queue that moves up or down one state at a time, while a detector records only some transitions. How much do the recorded totals fluctuate over a long observation period? For an infinite-state birth and death chain, this candidate gives an exact mathematical boundary. A series built from cumulative imbalance across the edges is finite precisely when the stationary variance grows at a finite asymptotic rate. If the series diverges, variance divided by time diverges too. When it is finite, the rescaled count process approaches Brownian motion from every fixed starting distribution. But there is an important distinction. Weak convergence does not automatically imply that variances converge. The paper constructs a starting distribution with infinite count variance at every positive time, even though the Brownian functional limit still holds. The result also allows finite detected activity when the mean rate of all underlying jumps is infinite. A joint-count extension handles several detectors whose decisions at the same jump may be correlated. Their individual detection probabilities do not determine their joint uncertainty; the simultaneous marking law matters. Earlier work already contains related cumulative-square criteria and general jump-count limit theorems. The contribution here is the stated infinite-state, integrability and marking scope, not the invention of that whole method. The package contains analytic proofs, worked examples and exact finite-state checks. These checks test formulas, not the entire infinite-state theorem. Released on 18 October 2026, this anonymous, AI-assisted candidate remains unrefereed. The paper and evidence are linked on Evidence Press. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
